extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; journalists interested in production routines
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the routine-based criteria that shape what gets defined and produced as news (event routines, intermedia influence, source routines, medium-specific constraints). Useful for analyzing or teaching news selection and production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event routine / Events define newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News is commonly thought to revolve around events; an 'event' routine helps organizations because events are more easily and less ambiguously defined as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events provide points of reference in time, let organizations schedule and allocate resources, and are 'defensible' as news. Television especially needs events because its visual nature 'demands that something happen.' Examples: coverage of train crashes abroad or distant apartment fires that fit the event model despite limited proxmity or importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event characteristics that increase media appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are visually and narratively compact are ideal news: clearly defined location and victim, dramatic elements (suffering, heroism, suspense), and an unambiguous life span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such features make stories easy to depict and time-bound (e.g., Jessica McClure 'baby in the well' rescue). Longer-term harms or issues without a compact event focus are less likely to receive the same coverage unless an event (operation, transplant) provides a peg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using event 'pegs' to frame issue stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Even general issue stories are often centered around a concrete news event 'peg' to give them a focus and schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists attach broader issues to a discrete occurrence to make them compatible with event-based news routines; this shapes which aspects of an issue are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermedia influence / Pack mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists rely heavily on each other and on other media for ideas and confirmation; consistency with peers provides certitude in an ambiguous environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'pack' follows wire services or dominant outlets to avoid editorial 'call-backs' and reduce risk. Studies show reporters often run with AP/UPI leads and monitor competitor leads as validation. Pack behavior is strongest on predictable beats and in crisis coverage when reliable information is scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency as an internal benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: Lacking firm external benchmarks, journalists take consistency (with other organizations and their own past work) as a guide to correct news judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic retrieval systems (e.g., Nexis) and past coverage make it easy to rely on previous stories; consistency reduces organizational risk and makes the product appear 'correct' to editors and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack coverage versus exclusives (scoop calculus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations balance the safety and affirmation of pack coverage against the prestige/performance value of exclusives or scoops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusives are rare and often aimed at competitive advantage or awards (e.g., Pulitzer); scoops serve as an easy-to-measure performance metric ('race for news'), but being too far ahead risks being wrong in view of the nation, so pack conformity often prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific constraint: television's visual and production demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Television's visual nature, smaller staffs, and production processes shape routines: need for visuals, use of 'standups', snappy language, less attribution, and fewer editorial layers for video packages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standups are recorded early and may lack later support; video is harder to change than copy, so TV reporters often depend on sources and PR control; broadcast reporters may be subordinated to sources and more dependent on news conferences and staged visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source reliance as a routinizing force
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations depend heavily on external suppliers (officials, press releases, interviews, hearings) for raw material; sources thereby dictate many routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases, press conferences, and photo ops make coverage more efficient but increase manipulability; rise of PR has routinized access and reduced scoops. Example: ~20% of press releases used verbatim in some outlets; press kits and handouts shape reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine channels taxonomy (official, informal, enterprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sigal's classification of information channels: routine channels (official proceedings, press releases, press conferences, nonspontaneous events), informal channels (background briefings, leaks, nongovernmental proceedings, other media reports), and enterprise channels (reporter-initiated interviews, firsthand spontaneous events, independent research, reporter analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical distributions show routine channels dominate (e.g., ~58% of front-page stories came from routine channels; Washington leads even higher). This taxonomy explains how channel choice shapes story content and perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-source control via press releases and press conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials prefer routine channels (press releases, conferences) that let them set rules and control information flow, often choreographing events and planting questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although press conferences appear adversarial, they are frequently scripted; friendly reporters recognized, hostile questions ignored, evasive answers given. This constrains journalistic ability to challenge or fully contextualize official claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background briefings and leak conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal briefings operate under conventions (off-the-record, deep background, background-only) that allow officials to provide information without standard attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters accept these terms to get information they otherwise wouldn't have; leaks (often targeted exclusives) serve tactical functions (float trial balloons, whistleblow, promote/sabotage policy, curry favor) and are routine tools for officials despite official complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts as routinized interpretive sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists routinely use a narrow, homogeneous, elite set of experts to contextualize events; experts are presented as objective and help create the 'illusion of objective reporting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts are valued for succinct, predictable, and centrist commentary that reduces need to balance; network news and major programs repeatedly use the same ~90 individuals, reinforcing conventional wisdom. Producers often select academics or think-tank analysts who will 'reinforce their own understanding' of a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency trade-offs: reliance on sources reduces research/specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependence on routine channels and sources lowers the need for expensive specialists and original research, shaping what gets reported and how deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This economizing makes reporting predictable and expedient but risks shallow or distorted views (e.g., lawsuit-based reporting favors plaintiffs' articulate lawyers; press-release reliance skews environmental coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source manipulation techniques ('scripted spontaneity' and access control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources (notably administrations) manipulate routines via staged events, restricting access, reducing unscripted encounters, and shaping visual opportunities to control the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include limiting press conferences, drowning out questions with noise, barring reporters from operations (e.g., Grenada), setting 'line of the day,' and planning headlines/pictures/leads in advance. These tactics increase media appetite for sanctioned information and reduce adversarial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and organizational incentives shaping routine adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational needs (scheduling, resource allocation, risk reduction, competition for audience or prizes) create incentives to adopt routinized practices like pack coverage, reliance on routine channels, and pursuit of scoops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News directors and editors plan around predictable events (e.g., annual meetings timed to avoid elections); reporters fear 'call-backs' and editors use consistency as shorthand for correctness; Pulitzer-oriented multipart series are exceptions driven by competitive goals.
